389|The **wild water buffalo** (_**Bubalus arnee**_), also called **Asian buffalo**, **Asiatic buffalo** and **wild buffalo**, is a large [bovine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bovinae "Bovinae") native to the [Indian subcontinent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_subcontinent "Indian subcontinent") and [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia"). It was first described in 1792.
390|
391|The wild water buffalo is the most likely ancestor of the domestic [water buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_buffalo "Water buffalo"). It has been listed as [endangered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endangered_species "Endangered species") on the [IUCN Red List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List "IUCN Red List") since 1986, as the global population totals less than 4,000 mature individuals.

393|## Taxonomy
394|
395|[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wild_water_buffalo&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Taxonomy")]

401|_Bos arnee_ was the [scientific name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_name "Scientific name") proposed by [Robert Kerr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Kerr_(writer) "Robert Kerr (writer)") in 1792 who described a skull with horns of a buffalo [zoological specimen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoological_specimen "Zoological specimen") from [Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal "Bengal") in northern India.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-Kerr-4)_Bubalus arnee_ was proposed by [Charles Hamilton Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Hamilton_Smith "Charles Hamilton Smith") in 1827 who introduced the generic name _Bubalus_ for bovids with large heads, convex-shaped narrow foreheads, laterally bent flat horns, funnel-shaped ears, small [dewlaps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewlap "Dewlap") and slender tails.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-5) Later authors subordinated the wild water buffalo under either _[Bos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bos "Bos")_, _Bubalus_ or _Buffelus_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-6)
402|
403|In 2003, the [International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Commission_on_Zoological_Nomenclature "International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature") placed _Bubalus arnee_ on the _Official List of [Specific Names](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specific\_name\_(zoology) "Specific name (zoology)") in Zoology_, recognizing the validity of this name for a wild species.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-7) Most authors have adopted the [binomen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomen "Binomen")_Bubalus arnee_ for the wild water buffalo as valid for the [taxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxon "Taxon").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-8)
404|
405|The wild water buffalo is the most likely ancestor of the domestic [water buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_buffalo "Water buffalo").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-Groves2006-10)
406|
407|Only a few [DNA sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_sequence "DNA sequence") are available from wild water buffalo populations.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-11) Wild populations are considered to be the [progenitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progenitor "Progenitor") of the modern domestic water buffalo, but the [genetic variation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_variation "Genetic variation") within the species is unclear, and also how it is related to the domesticated river and [Carabao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carabao "Carabao") swamp buffaloes.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-12)

409|## Etymology
410|

413|The specific name _arnee_ is reminiscent of the classical [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") word _arnī_ meaning female wild buffalo.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-13)
414|
415|## Characteristics
416|
417|[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wild_water_buffalo&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Characteristics")]
418|
419|[![Image 23](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Bubalus_arnee_schaedel.JPG/250px-Bubalus_arnee_schaedel.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bubalus_arnee_schaedel.JPG)
420|
421|Skull of a wild water buffalo in the [Bavarian State Collection of Zoology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_State_Collection_of_Zoology "Bavarian State Collection of Zoology")
422|
423|The wild water buffalo has an ash-gray to black skin. The moderately long, coarse and sparse hair is directed forward from the haunches to the long and narrow head. There is a tuft on the forehead, and the ears are comparatively small. Its head-to-body-length is 240 to 300 cm (94 to 118 in) with a 60 to 100 cm (24 to 39 in) long tail and a shoulder height of 150 to 190 cm (59 to 75 in). Both sexes carry horns that are heavy at the base and widely spreading up to 2 m (6 ft 7 in) along the outer edges, exceeding in size the horns of any other living [bovid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bovid "Bovid"). The tip of the tail is bushy; the hooves are large and splayed.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-Nowak99-14) It is larger and heavier than the domestic water buffalo, and weighs from 600 to 1,200 kg (1,300 to 2,600 lb).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-Aryal2011-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-Ahrestani2016-16) The average weight of three captive wild water buffaloes was 900 kg (2,000 lb).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-17) It is among the heaviest living wild bovid species, and is slightly smaller than [gaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaur "Gaur").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-18)
424|
425|## Distribution and habitat
426|
427|[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wild_water_buffalo&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Distribution and habitat")]
428|
429|The wild water buffalo occurs in India, [Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal"), [Bhutan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhutan "Bhutan"), [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand"), and [Cambodia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodia "Cambodia"), with an unconfirmed population in [Myanmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myanmar "Myanmar"). It has been [extirpated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_extinction "Local extinction") in Bangladesh, [Laos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laos "Laos"), [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam "Vietnam") and [Sri Lanka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Lanka "Sri Lanka").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-iucn-2)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-Choudhury2010-19) It inhabits wet grasslands, swamps, flood plains and densely vegetated river valleys.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-iucn-2)
430|
431|In India, it is largely restricted to in and around [Kaziranga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaziranga_National_Park "Kaziranga National Park"), [Manas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manas_National_Park "Manas National Park") and [Dibru-Saikhowa National Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dibru-Saikhowa_National_Park "Dibru-Saikhowa National Park"), [Laokhowa Wildlife Sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laokhowa_Wildlife_Sanctuary "Laokhowa Wildlife Sanctuary") and [Bura Chapori Wildlife Sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bura_Chapori_Wildlife_Sanctuary "Bura Chapori Wildlife Sanctuary") and in a few scattered pockets in Assam, and in and around [D'Ering Memorial Wildlife Sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D'Ering_Memorial_Wildlife_Sanctuary "D'Ering Memorial Wildlife Sanctuary") in Arunachal Pradesh. A small population survives in [Balphakram National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balphakram_National_Park "Balphakram National Park") in Meghalaya, and in [Chhattisgarh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chhattisgarh "Chhattisgarh") in [Indravati National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indravati_National_Park "Indravati National Park") and [Udanti Wildlife Sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Udanti_Wildlife_Sanctuary "Udanti Wildlife Sanctuary").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-Choudhury2010-19) This population might extend into adjacent parts of [Odisha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odisha,_India "Odisha, India"). In the early 1990s, there may still have been about 3,300–3,500 wild water buffaloes in Assam and the adjacent states of northeast India.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-Choudhury94-20) In 1997, the number was assessed at less than 1,500 mature individuals.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-iucn-2)
432|
433|[![Image 24](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/Asiatic_buffalo.jpg/250px-Asiatic_buffalo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Asiatic_buffalo.jpg)
434|
435|A herd of wild water buffaloes in Kaziranga National Park, Assam
436|
437|Many surviving populations are thought to have interbred with [feral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feral "Feral") or domestic water buffaloes. In the late 1980s, fewer than 100 wild water buffaloes were left in [Madhya Pradesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madhya_Pradesh "Madhya Pradesh").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-21) By 1992, only 50 animals were estimated to have survived there.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-Choudhury94-20)
438|
439|Nepal's only population lives in [Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koshi_Tappu_Wildlife_Reserve "Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve") and has grown from 63 individuals in 1976 to 219 individuals in 2009.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-22) In 2016, 18 individuals were translocated from Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve to [Chitwan National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chitwan_National_Park "Chitwan National Park").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-23)
440|
441|[![Image 25](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Wild_water_buffalo_at_Koshi_Tappu_Wildlife_Reserve.jpg/250px-Wild_water_buffalo_at_Koshi_Tappu_Wildlife_Reserve.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wild_water_buffalo_at_Koshi_Tappu_Wildlife_Reserve.jpg)
442|
443|Wild water buffalo at Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve, Nepal
444|
445|In and around Bhutan's [Royal Manas National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Manas_National_Park "Royal Manas National Park"), a small number of wild water buffaloes occur. This is part of the sub-population that occurs in India's Manas National Park.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-Choudhury2010-19) In Myanmar, a few animals live in [Hukaung Valley Wildlife Sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hukaung_Valley_Wildlife_Sanctuary "Hukaung Valley Wildlife Sanctuary").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-iucn-2)
446|
447|In Thailand, wild water buffaloes have been reported to occur in small herds of less than 40 individuals. A population of 25–60 individuals inhabited lowland areas of the [Huai Kha Khaeng Wildlife Sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huai_Kha_Khaeng_Wildlife_Sanctuary "Huai Kha Khaeng Wildlife Sanctuary") between December 1999 and April 2001. This population has not grown significantly in 15 years, and is maybe interbreeding with domestic water buffaloes.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-24)
448|
449|The population in Cambodia is confined to a small area of easternmost [Mondulkiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mondulkiri_Province "Mondulkiri Province") and possibly [Ratanakiri Provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratanakiri_Province "Ratanakiri Province"). Only a few dozen individuals remained as of 2005.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-25)
450|
451|The wild water buffaloes in [Sri Lanka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Lanka "Sri Lanka") are thought to be descendants of the introduced domestic [water buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_buffalo "Water buffalo"). It is unlikely that any true wild water buffaloes remain there today.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-iucn-2) Wild-living populations found elsewhere in Asia, Australia, [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina") and [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") are [feral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feral "Feral") domestic water buffaloes.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-Nowak99-14)
452|
453|## Ecology and behaviour
454|
455|[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wild_water_buffalo&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Ecology and behaviour")]
456|
457|[![Image 26](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Indian_Water_Buffalo_Bubalus_arnee_by_Dr_Raju_Kasambe_IMG_0347_%2812%29.JPG/250px-Indian_Water_Buffalo_Bubalus_arnee_by_Dr_Raju_Kasambe_IMG_0347_%2812%29.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Indian_Water_Buffalo_Bubalus_arnee_by_Dr_Raju_Kasambe_IMG_0347_(12).JPG)
458|
459|Water buffalo fighting
460|
461|The wild water buffalo is both [diurnal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diurnality "Diurnality") and [nocturnal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nocturnal "Nocturnal"). Adult females and their young form stable clans of as many as 30 individuals, which have [home ranges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_range "Home range") of 170 to 1,000 ha (420 to 2,470 acres) that include areas for resting, grazing, wallowing and drinking. Clans are led by old cows, even when bulls accompany the group. Several clans form a herd of 30 to 500 animals that gather at resting areas. Adult males form bachelor groups of up to 10 individuals, with older males often being solitary, and spend the dry season apart from the female clans. They are seasonal breeders in most of their range, typically in October and November. However, some populations breed year round. Dominant males mate with the females of a clan who subsequently drive them off. Their [gestation period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gestation_period "Gestation period") is 10 to 11 months, with an inter-birth interval of one year. They typically give birth to a single offspring, although twins are possible. Age at sexual maturity is 18 months for males, and three years for females. The maximum known lifespan is 25 years in the wild.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-Nowak99-14) In Assam, herd sizes vary from three to 30 individuals.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-Choudhury2010-19)
462|
463|The wild water buffalo is probably a [grazer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grazing "Grazing") by preference, feeding mainly on [graminoids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graminoid "Graminoid") when available, such as [Bermuda grass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynodon_dactylon "Cynodon dactylon"), and _[Cyperus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyperus "Cyperus")_ sedges, but it also eats other [herbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbaceous_plant "Herbaceous plant"), fruits, and bark, and [browses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Browsing_(predation) "Browsing (predation)") on trees and shrubs.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-26) It also feeds on crops, including rice, [sugarcane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarcane "Sugarcane"), and [jute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jute "Jute"), sometimes causing considerable damage.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-27) During the [Pleistocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleistocene "Pleistocene"), its diet was far more varied; it foraged in C 3-dominant forests and woodlands and in C 4-dominant grasslands, while today it is restricted to the latter type of environment.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-28)
464|
465|[Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger "Tiger") and [mugger crocodiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugger_crocodile "Mugger crocodile") prey on adult wild water buffaloes, and [Asian black bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_black_bear "Asian black bear") have also been known to kill them.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-29)
466|
467|## Threats
468|
469|[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wild_water_buffalo&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Threats")]
470|
471|A population reduction by at least 50% over the last three generations seems likely given the severity of the threats, especially [hybridization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hybrid_(biology) "Hybrid (biology)"); this population trend is projected to continue into the future. The most important threats are:[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-iucn-2)
472|
473|*   [interbreeding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interbreeding "Interbreeding") with feral and domestic water buffaloes in and around protected areas;
474|*   hunting, especially in Thailand, Cambodia, and Myanmar;
475|*   habitat loss of [floodplain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floodplain "Floodplain") areas due to conversion to agriculture and [hydropower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydropower "Hydropower") development;
476|*   degradation of [wetlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wetlands "Wetlands") due to [invasive species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasive_species "Invasive species") such as [stem twiners and lianas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikania "Mikania");
477|*   diseases and [parasites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasites "Parasites") transmitted by domestic livestock;
478|*   [interspecific competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interspecific_competition "Interspecific competition") for food and water between wild water buffaloes and livestock.
479|
480|## Conservation
481|
482|[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wild_water_buffalo&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Conservation")]
483|
484|_Bubalus arnee_ is included in [CITES Appendix III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CITES_Appendix_III "CITES Appendix III"), and is legally protected in Bhutan, India, Nepal, and Thailand.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-iucn-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-CITES-3)
485|
486|In 2017, 15 wild water buffaloes were [reintroduced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reintroduced "Reintroduced") into [Chitwan National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chitwan_National_Park "Chitwan National Park") in Nepal to establish a second viable sub-population in the country.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-30)
487|
488|In 2023, four wild buffalos were translocated to Udanti-Sitanadi Tiger Reserve to reverse its declining population in the state.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_water_buffalo#cite_note-31)

It is hoped, with this Threatened Species List, that the huge hidden information base held at the lUCN Conservation Monitoring Centre may be exposed to a wider audience.
There is, of course, an inherent problem with any data base of any quality and size; everybody wants access to it instantly, but the reality is that all this hard won information has got to be distilled, manipulated and reproduced in a particular format for any user.
This takes time and time is money, so by exposing the data base one is apparently issuing an invitation to use it, whereas I think we should all be aware that to use it means we have to find the money to pay for its use.
It cannot be provided for free!
The great skills of the staff and the huge network of specialists from which the data is acquired, many of whom are members of the Specialist Groups of the Species Survival Commission, are actually worth paying for, painful as this concept might be.
It was with great pleasure that World Wildlife Fund UK agreed to pay for the publication of this species list, to show what the data base holds and, to show the status of the species held, which in itself is of value to a whole range of users.
As one reviews, during this 25th Anniversary Year of the World Wildlife Fund, what has been accomplished in species conservation, it must be said that whilst we have done well in creating an extensive information base, we are sadly still very far away from being in a position to have plans and programmes to ensure the wise management of all these threatened species.
Our success in the field and 'in captivity' sometimes obscures this reality!
The reality, in fact, shows the need for greater and more vigorous action but, having said this, I believe we should congratulate the team at the Conservation Monitoring Centre for their sterling effort in the battle for species conservation.

Lucas, Chairman, Species Survival Commission, lUCN 28th August, 1986 CONTENTS Page Introduction iii Inventory Report Form v Documents on which the lUCN Red List is based vii Taxonomy viii lUCN Category Definitions ix List of Abbreviations x Threatened Species List Mammals 2 Birds 15 Reptiles 33 Amphibians 38 Fishes 39 Invertebrates 49 Index 97 Introduction lUCN has long been known for the compilation of a series of Red Data Books, authoritative international inventories of threatened species.
In recent years the Red Data Books have changed in format from the original loose-leaf style which allowed for frequent update of species accounts, to that of bound volumes.
In addition, some books have become regional rather than global in approach, e.g. Threatened Birds of Africa and Related Islands.
As a result, a list of internationally threatened species has not been readily available from lUCN for some years.
This publication has been prepared in response to the increasing demand for such a list, from scientists, educationalists, zoos, the media, and conservation organisations.
It is intended that new editions of the list will be published periodically.
The Red Data Book concept, originated by Sir Peter Scott in the mid-1960s, aimed to focus attention on the plight of the earth's vanishing wildlife.
The concept has been immensely successful and, two decades later, many national and regional Red Datc^ Books have been published; and many more countries are in the process of compiling their own threatened species lists.
National and regional compilations are always likely to be more detailed than the international overview provided by lUCN.
Increasingly therefore, lUCN's role will be to provide pointers to the availability of such data sources.
Where these exist, lUCN will not duplicate the detailed information they contain, but will list any identified globally threatened taxa on its international list.
For example, Australia has in recent years produced several texts detailing the status of its native species.
lUCN will include all the relevant threateneu Australian species on the international list but will not give high priority to the compilation of detailed data sheets for Australian taxa.
The next generation of Red Data Books prepared by lUCN will thus tend to be shorter, more specific publications highlighting the conservation problems of a group of species, perhaps even a single species, or an area.
Such shorter compilations will allow for faster dissemination of conservation data, and will be more responsive to the changing priorities and needs of conservation.
Complementing these, the periodic publication of the lUCN list of internationally threatened species will provide an index to the species data held by lUCN.
lUCN's threatened species list is compiled and maintained by the lUCN Conservation Monitoring Centre.
For each threatened taxon, the list provides the scientific name, English vernacular name (where known), lUCN category (for definitions see page ix), and a brief description of the animal's distribution.
This is followed by an index to the list based on the order, family and generic listing.
Vernacular names for major groupings such as monkeys, parrots, and butterflies are also included.
Data upon which the listings are made are gathered from literature searches, and from correspondence with specialists around the world, including those belonging to the Specialist Groups of lUCN's Species Survival Commission.
-Ill-The number of threatened animal taxa identified by lUCN is 3117, comprised of 385 mammals, 428 birds, 143 reptiles, 46 amphibians, 286 fishes, and 1829 invertebrates.
These numbers, however, represent only those taxa whose threatened status has been brought to the attention of lUCN; many, many more taxa, particularly invertebrates are threatened, and going extinct every year unbeknownst to the scientific and conservation communities.
Thus the number of threatened taxa identified by lUCN represents only the visible fraction of a much greater problem.
The vertebrate listings are based almost entirely on the lUCN Red Data Books.
For invertebrates, however, it must be stressed that the list is only provisional, since most species have not yet been subjected to the same review process as has been carried out for the vertebrate groups, apart from those listed in the lUCN Invertebrate Red Data Book and Swallowtail Butterfly Red Data Book.
Other invertebrate listings have been taken from correspondence and a number of published sources (noted on page vii).
The threatened species list is constantly under review; as new areas or species groups are surveyed, species may be listed or delisted or categories may change.
Since at any one time work is focused on a particular group of species, some parts of the list are more up to date than others.
For example, a review of the conservation status of the birds of Africa and related islands was undertaken by lUCN and ICBP (the International Council for Bird Preservation) between 1982 and 1985, leading to the publication of the Bird Red Data Book for Africa.
Work is now in progress to assess the conservation status of the birds of the Americas.
Information on Asian birds has not therefore been reviewed for some time (although files and correspondence are maintained), and so changes are undoubtedly required.
The need for new information is thus continuous and assistance in providing accurate data always welcome. An inventory report form is detailed on page v and is a guide to the information required by lUCN to assess the international conservation status of a species.

The **yellow-eared parrot** (***Ognorhynchus icterotis***) is a [vulnerable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulnerable_species "Vulnerable species") [parrot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parrot "Parrot") found in the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") of [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia"). It was thought to be extinct up until April 1999, when a group of researchers that were sponsored by ABC and Fundación Loro Parque, discovered a total of 81 individuals in the Colombian Andes.[[3]](#cite_note-3) It is currently enlisted as [vulnerable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulnerable_species "Vulnerable species") on the [International Union for Conservation of Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Union_for_Conservation_of_Nature "International Union for Conservation of Nature") (IUCN) Red List. Its current population trend is increasing, in part due to conservation measures implemented to protect the existing populations of the species. It is closely associated with the wax palm (*[Ceroxylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceroxylon "Ceroxylon")* sp.).

## Description

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Yellow-eared_parrot&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Description")]

The yellow-eared parrot is a relatively large, long-tailed parrot, with an average length of 42 cm (17 in) and a weight of about 285 g (10.1 oz).[[4]](#cite_note-4) It is overall green, with the underparts being paler, more [lime green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lime_(color) "Lime (color)") than the upperparts. The heavy beak and a ring of bare skin around the eyes are black. The origin of the common epithet "yellow-eared" derives from the yellow patch of feathers that extends from the forehead down to its cheeks and ear-coverts. Its calls sound similar to those of geese.[[5]](#cite_note-ourendangeredworld.com-5)

120|The **yellow-eared parrot** (***Ognorhynchus icterotis***) is a [vulnerable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulnerable_species "Vulnerable species") [parrot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parrot "Parrot") found in the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") of [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia"). It was thought to be extinct up until April 1999, when a group of researchers that were sponsored by ABC and Fundación Loro Parque, discovered a total of 81 individuals in the Colombian Andes.[[3]](#cite_note-3) It is currently enlisted as [vulnerable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulnerable_species "Vulnerable species") on the [International Union for Conservation of Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Union_for_Conservation_of_Nature "International Union for Conservation of Nature") (IUCN) Red List. Its current population trend is increasing, in part due to conservation measures implemented to protect the existing populations of the species. It is closely associated with the wax palm (*[Ceroxylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceroxylon "Ceroxylon")* sp.).
121|
122|## Description
123|
124|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Yellow-eared_parrot&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Description")]
125|
126|The yellow-eared parrot is a relatively large, long-tailed parrot, with an average length of 42 cm (17 in) and a weight of about 285 g (10.1 oz).[[4]](#cite_note-4) It is overall green, with the underparts being paler, more [lime green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lime_(color) "Lime (color)") than the upperparts. The heavy beak and a ring of bare skin around the eyes are black. The origin of the common epithet "yellow-eared" derives from the yellow patch of feathers that extends from the forehead down to its cheeks and ear-coverts. Its calls sound similar to those of geese.[[5]](#cite_note-ourendangeredworld.com-5)
127|
128|## Distribution and habitat
129|
130|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Yellow-eared_parrot&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Distribution and habitat")]
131|
132|The yellow-eared parrot nests and lives among [wax palms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceroxylon "Ceroxylon") in a few areas of [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Occidental_(Colombia) "Cordillera Occidental (Colombia)") and [Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_Central_(Colombia) "Cordillera Central (Colombia)") cordilleras of [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia"), which are northern sub-ranges of the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes"), where it inhabits cloud forests about 1800–3000 meters above sea level. It nests in the hollow trunks of the palms, usually 25–30 meters over the floor level. It also occurred very locally in northern [Ecuador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuador "Ecuador"). Its numbers have been greatly reduced, and only 81 individuals were recorded in the Colombian census of 1999. Their populations have been impacted by hunting and [habitat destruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitat_destruction "Habitat destruction"), particularly the harvesting of wax palm, which was traditionally cut down and used each year on [Palm Sunday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palm_Sunday "Palm Sunday"). There has been no confirmed record of this parrot from Ecuador since the mid-1990s. The number of mature individuals in the population is 212, though it is thought that there is a total of 1,408 individuals in the wild.[[1]](#cite_note-iucn_status_20_November_2021-1)
133|
134|It is also found in [Riosucio, Caldas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riosucio,_Caldas "Riosucio, Caldas") in Colombia.
135|
136|[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Colwachspalme01.jpg/250px-Colwachspalme01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Colwachspalme01.jpg)
137|
138|Panorama of the [Cocora valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocora_Valley "Cocora Valley") with wax palms
139|
140|## Ecology
141|
142|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Yellow-eared_parrot&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Ecology")]
143|
144|### Diet
145|
146|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Yellow-eared_parrot&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Diet")]
147|
148|Yellow-eared parrots rely on the wax palm for much of their life cycle. One of their principle foods is the [wax palm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceroxylon "Ceroxylon") fruit, although they will eat other fruits and seeds as well, plus bark, buds and ferns. They nest in these trees because of their hollow trunks, which is about 30 meters above the forest floor, making their habitat in the [cloud forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_forest "Cloud forest") and [elfin forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elfin_forest "Elfin forest") of Colombia.[[5]](#cite_note-ourendangeredworld.com-5)
149|
150|### Breeding
151|
152|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Yellow-eared_parrot&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Breeding")]
153|
154|Yellow-eared parrots tend to be social birds who gather in flocks of about one to two dozen at times. Several of these parrots tend to cooperate in rearing chicks which increases their chances of survival. These birds can have up to two broods of young per year.[[5]](#cite_note-ourendangeredworld.com-5)
155|
156|## Conservation threats to habitat
157|
158|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Yellow-eared_parrot&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Conservation threats to habitat")]
159|
160|The yellow-eared parrot has suffered greatly from [habitat fragmentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitat_fragmentation "Habitat fragmentation") and habitat loss. Specifically, over 90-93% of montane forests in Colombia have been cleared for agricultural use or settlement.[[1]](#cite_note-iucn_status_20_November_2021-1) Sizable areas of its historical habitat remain, which adds to its decline, as the current habitat is what is suffering the most. The Quindio wax palm (*[Ceroxylon quindiuense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceroxylon_quindiuense "Ceroxylon quindiuense")*), is a species of palm that is native to the humid montane forests of the Andes in Colombia. The yellow-eared parrot depends greatly on the Quindio wax palm for roosting, nesting, and feeding on its fruits, where it nests usually 25–30 meters over the floor level in the trunk. This palm species has become highly threatened due to the use of its fronds to adorn Palm Sunday processions.[[6]](#cite_note-datazone.birdlife.org-6) Some other threats include residential and commercial development such as housing and urban areas, as well as logging and wood harvesting.
161|
162|## Use and trade
163|
164|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Yellow-eared_parrot&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Use and trade")]
165|
166|The yellow-eared parrot is hunted for food at the local and national level. At the international level, the use of these parrots as pets or as display animals has contributed to this species decline. The parrot had previously been hunted for food, especially in Ecuador, which is why there are so few to none of these individuals found in Ecuador today.[[1]](#cite_note-iucn_status_20_November_2021-1)
167|
168|## Conservation actions in place
169|
170|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Yellow-eared_parrot&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Conservation actions in place")]
171|
172|From 1998, [Fundación ProAves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundación_ProAves "Fundación ProAves") with the support of [Fundacion Loro Parque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundacion_Loro_Parque "Fundacion Loro Parque"), [American Bird Conservancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bird_Conservancy "American Bird Conservancy"), CORANTIOQUIA, and local environmentalists like Gonzalo Cardona Molina[[7]](#cite_note-7) have undertaken an intensive conservation project across Colombia that has led to one of Latin America's most successful recoveries of an endangered bird. As a result of the initial finding of this small population, Fundación ProAves Yellow-eared Parrot Bird Reserve has been founded to focus on recovering this species, along with the wax palm. Currently in Colombia, there are awareness raising events to reduce hunting pressure and the impact of Palm Sunday processions which involve poster campaigns, environmental education, community workshops, school visits, and radio.
173|
174|A publicity campaign, which included television and radio appeals, music concerts and a touring 'Parrot Bus' made for a huge increase in awareness of the problems facing the parrot and its habitat throughout Colombia.[[6]](#cite_note-datazone.birdlife.org-6) This campaign grew into an alliance of over 35 national NGOs, government departments, and the Episcopal Conference of Colombia. Through the endorsement by the Catholic Church, an end was brought to the use of wax palm fronds for Palm Sunday across a large part of the country of Colombia, and sustainable alternatives were promoted instead.
175|
176|A significant increase in the population can be attributed to the implementation of fencing and breeding sites to allow wax palm regeneration and habitat restoration and provision of artificial nest boxes. The Fundación ProAves owns two reserves where conservation efforts are focused on this species, one near Jardín and the other in Roncesvalles-Tolima. In 2009, ProAves, the Loro Parque Fundación, the American Bird Conservancy and others established a corridor of over 16,000 acres (including the acquisition of over 10,000 acres) for the Yellow-eared Parrot and other threatened parrots across the Central Cordillera in Colombia. Artificial nests have also been implemented in San Luis de Cubarral in 2011. With protection and community support, the yellow-eared parrot population has climbed to over 1500 individuals by 2012, with one of the most successful recovery projects for an endangered bird.[[1]](#cite_note-iucn_status_20_November_2021-1) In the future, searching for additional populations will become very important, especially for possible populations in Ecuador. There has also been talk of purchasing and protecting further habitats in these regions, along with making wax palm nurseries in order to replant those that were destroyed.[[1]](#cite_note-iucn_status_20_November_2021-1)
177|
178|In 2021, Sara Inés Lara, executive director of Fundación ProAves and Women for Conservation, spoke at L'Oréal - [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO") For Women in Science festival[[8]](#cite_note-8) about the conservation of Yellow-eared Parrots. At this event forty women researchers shared their inspiring stories about how they are changing the world through their loves for science and the environment. Sara Inés Lara spoke about the impactful work ProAves has done in order to take the 81 individual Yellow-eared Parrots that remained in 1999 to over 3,000 individuals that remain today. ProAves partnered with Women for Conservation not only to protect the Yellow-eared Parrot through maternal action, but also to provide sustainable livelihoods to women in Colombia. Women for Conservation establish women community networks around the 28 Fundación ProAves reserves through entrepreneur workshops, environmental education, family planning programs, and training as reserve rangers.
179|
180|## Conservation research needed
181|
182|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Yellow-eared_parrot&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Conservation research needed")]
183|
184|The conservation actions that are still needed is continued resource and habitat protection. This would include buying and protecting further habitat. Also, the continuation of species recovery by continuing the current highly successful programme of conservation activities in Colombia, along with extending these activities to Ecuador to any sub populations that are identified within Ecuador in the future.[[1]](#cite_note-iucn_status_20_November_2021-1)
185|
186|The research that is still needed includes population, size, distribution, and trends. This means that search for additional populations is needed, with a focus on determining status within the Intag Valley in Ecuador, and prepare habitat maps of the Volcán Ruiz-Tolima massif, which is a group of five ice-capped volcanoes which includes the Tolima, Santa Isabel, Quindio and Machin volcanoes.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]
187|

287|#### Justification
288|
289|_**Criterion A: Population Reduction**_ Following the IUCN guidelines, we determined the overall abundance loss for this species by weighting factors. We include estimates reported in points 1–4 in the _Population_ section (below) by region (see Tables 1–3 in the additional supporting information). All range areas are calculated as extent of occurrence (EOO). Data limitations precluded us from estimating aquatic habitat area.
290|
291|Most of the historic range of the species is contained in the Russian Federation (83.8% of total). The species' historic, natural range extends into China (6.4% of total), Kazakhstan (6.1% of total) and Mongolia (3.7% of total; see Table 1 in the additional supporting information).
292|
293|We estimate a total natural range reduction of 3.6% (see Table 1 in the additional supporting information). Loss in range area for specific regions varies from 3.2% within Russia (in the Volga, Ural and Pechora Rivers), 6.9% within China (in the Amur River basin), and 19.1% within Mongolia (see Table 2 in the additional supporting information). We acknowledge that percentage loss of range calculated as area of occupancy (AOO) would likely be much higher than this, considering many populations, particularly along the southern extent of their distribution, have become significantly fragmented as a result of localized impacts from land use change and fishing pressure. However, we lack the data to generate reliable estimates of AOO for this species throughout most of its natural range.
294|
295|To arrive at a population reduction estimate for this species to evaluate it against IUCN Red List Criterion A, we used our abundance loss estimates for each region (described in points 1–4 in the _Population_ section below), weighted by the percent of the range in each region, as prescribed by the _Guidelines for Using the IUCN Red List Categories and Criteria_ (Version 9.0; see Table 3 in the additional supporting information). We were unable to obtain an estimate of population trend within Kazakhstan, so we excluded this region from our range-wide analysis. The analysis yielded a population reduction of 37.3% (see Table 3 in the additional supporting information). It is important to acknowledge that this estimate is influenced most significantly by the abundance reduction we applied to the majority of the species' range in Russia (Volga, Ural, and the Arctic and Sea of Okhotsk river drainages; see Table 3 in the additional supporting information).
296|
297|Based on criterion A2, this results in a status of VU (Vulnerable) for this species, based on A2b (index of abundance appropriate to the taxon), A2c (a decline in AOO, EOO and/or habitat quality), and A2d (actual or potential levels of exploitation).
298|
299|_**Criterion B: Geographic Range and Continuing Decline**_ We estimated the total historic range (EOO) to be 12,404,332 km² (including the entire watershed area). The total range area lost is estimated to be 444,972 km². Since the species' range estimates are well outside the thresholds used for IUCN Red List Criterion B, this species does not qualify for listing under this criterion.
300|
301|**_Criteria C and D: Current Population Size_**No estimates are available for current population size, therefore the species does not qualify for listing under criterion C or D. Also, the species' range is not sufficiently restricted to qualify it for listing under VU D2.
302|
303|_**Criterion D: Quantitative Analysis**_ Insufficient data are available to carry out a quantitative analysis to estimate the probability of extinction for this species. Therefore criterion E cannot be used in this case.

349|#### Range Description
350|
351|The Siberian Taimen occurs in Europe and Asia, including parts of the Caspian and Arctic drainages in Eurasia (Volga, Ural, Pechora, Yenisey, Lena) and portions of the Pacific drainage in Mongolia, Russia, and China. The western border of their natural range is upstream reaches of the Volga and Pechora Rivers. The species is found in a number of tributaries of Pechora, including Ilych, Kosiu, Bolshaia Synia, and Usa. There have been no records of presence of this fish in Komi Republic for the last 20 years; the last reported catch of the species in the Komi Republic was in the Ilych River in 1978 (Taskaev 2009). Much of the range within the Volga and Ural Rivers (including the Malyi Ik River tributary) has been lost. The only place in Europe where the species is still present is the Kama River (particularly the Vishera River), where there is still a limited fishery. 285|#### Justification
286|
287|_**Criterion A: Population Reduction**_ Following the IUCN guidelines, we determined the overall abundance loss for this species by weighting factors. We include estimates reported in points 1–4 in the _Population_ section (below) by region (see Tables 1–3 in the Supplementary Material). All range areas are calculated as extent of occurrence (EOO). Data limitations precluded us from estimating aquatic habitat area.
288|
289|Most of the historic range of the species is contained in the Russian Federation (83.8% of total). The species' historic, natural range extends into China (6.4% of total), Kazakhstan (6.1% of total) and Mongolia (3.7% of total; see Table 1 in the Supplementary Material).
290|
291|We estimate a total natural range reduction of 3.6% (see Table 1 in the Supplementary Material). Loss in range area for specific regions varies from 3.2% within Russia (in the Volga, Ural and Pechora Rivers), 6.9% within China (in the Amur River basin), and 19.1% within Mongolia (see Table 2 in the Supplementary Material). We acknowledge that percentage loss of range calculated as area of occupancy (AOO) would likely be much higher than this, considering many populations, particularly along the southern extent of their distribution, have become significantly fragmented as a result of localized impacts from land use change and fishing pressure. However, we lack the data to generate reliable estimates of AOO for this species throughout most of its natural range.
292|
293|To arrive at a population reduction estimate for this species to evaluate it against IUCN Red List Criterion A, we used our abundance loss estimates for each region (described in points 1–4 in the _Population_ section below), weighted by the percent of the range in each region, as prescribed by the _Guidelines for Using the IUCN Red List Categories and Criteria_ (Version 9.0; see Table 3 in the Supplementary Material). We were unable to obtain an estimate of population trend within Kazakhstan, so we excluded this region from our range-wide analysis. The analysis yielded a population reduction of 37.3% (see Table 3 in the Supplementary Material). It is important to acknowledge that this estimate is influenced most significantly by the abundance reduction we applied to the majority of the species' range in Russia (Volga, Ural, and the Arctic and Sea of Okhotsk river drainages; see Table 3 in the Supplementary Material).
294|
295|Based on criterion A2, this results in a status of VU (Vulnerable) for this species, based on A2b (index of abundance appropriate to the taxon), A2c (a decline in AOO, EOO and/or habitat quality), and A2d (actual or potential levels of exploitation).
296|
297|_**Criterion B: Geographic Range and Continuing Decline**_ We estimated the total historic range (EOO) to be 12,404,332 km² (including the entire watershed area). The total range area lost is estimated to be 444,972 km². Since the species' range estimates are well outside the thresholds used for IUCN Red List Criterion B, this species does not qualify for listing under this criterion.
298|
299|**_Criteria C and D: Current Population Size_**No estimates are available for current population size, therefore the species does not qualify for listing under criterion C or D. Also, the species' range is not sufficiently restricted to qualify it for listing under VU D2.
300|
301|_**Criterion D: Quantitative Analysis**_ Insufficient data are available to carry out a quantitative analysis to estimate the probability of extinction for this species. Therefore criterion E cannot be used in this case.

345|#### Range Description
346|
347|The Siberian Taimen occurs in Europe and Asia, including parts of the Caspian and Arctic drainages in Eurasia (Volga, Ural, Pechora, Yenisey, Lena) and portions of the Pacific drainage in Mongolia, Russia, and China. The western border of their natural range is upstream reaches of the Volga and Pechora Rivers. The species is found in a number of tributaries of Pechora, including Ilych, Kosiu, Bolshaia Synia, and Usa. There have been no records of presence of this fish in Komi Republic for the last 20 years; the last reported catch of the species in the Komi Republic was in the Ilych River in 1978 (Taskaev 2009). Much of the range within the Volga and Ural Rivers (including the Malyi Ik River tributary) has been lost. The only place in Europe where the species is still present is the Kama River (particularly the Vishera River), where there is still a limited fishery. The Siberian Taimen is also present in Yaiva River, and there are also records in Kosva, Chusovaia and Beryozovaia Rivers (Melnikova 1998). The species was observed in 1987 in Udmurtia Republic, in the Siva River and the downstream section of the Votkono reservoir (Tepliakov 2002). It is found in Khabarovsk Krai, including Amur River and its tributaries and the Tugur and Uda Rivers along the Sea of Okhotsk coast (Zolotukhin et al. 2000). The species has been occasionally collected in the Langry River in northern Sakhalin Island (Safronov et al. 1998, Semenchenko and Zolotukhin 2011). In Mongolia, the Siberian Taimen is found in the Shiskhed, Eg, Uur, Delger Moron, Ider, Chuluud, Eroo, Selenge, Orkhon, and Tuul rivers, and Darkhad Depression (Arctic drainage), and Onon, upper Kherlen and Khalkhin rivers (Amur drainage). In China, it occurs in the Heilongjiang (Amur) River and its tributary the Eerqisi as well as the headwaters of the Irtysh River in the Altai region in Xinjiang Province. 
348|
349|See Figure 1 in the Supplementary Material for a map of the historic and current distribution of the species. This species has been listed as Endangered in country Red Lists and regional Red Books (see Figure 2 in the Supplementary Material).

Data are reported as weight (in MT) of landed biomass of Siberian Taimen. It is important to note here that reporting of catch over this entire period has not been consistent, and much of the catch has gone unreported, particularly in recent decades. 420|

424|
425|Abundance of _H. taimen_ in most of this region has been declining (primarily from unregulated catch, both commercial and recreational), but there are no reliable indices of adult abundance trends to quantify the decline in a rigorous manner.
426|
427|A review of Siberian Taimen status was conducted in 57 river basins within the Russian Federation (including the Amur River, M. Skopets, unpublished data). Populations were divided into four categories: nearly extirpated, significant decline (i.e., more than 50%), moderate decline (i.e., between 30–50%), and healthy (less than 30%). Skopets found that Siberian Taimen populations have been extirpated or have undergone significant decline in 39 of 57 river basins and only a few populations could be still considered stable, primarily due to their remote, inaccessible locations. Skopets categorized Taimen populations as being at moderate risk in over half of Russian river basins and at high risk in all rivers west of the Ural mountains. Even in some very remote areas (such as mountainous rivers of the Urals) Siberian Taimen populations have declined by over 50% (M. Skopets, pers. comm).
428|

Knizhin, Irkutsk State University, pers. comm). The actual level of exploitation (illegal harvest) is thought to be significant throughout this region. The species is expected to continue to decline by at least 30% over the next three generations (51 years) within this region (I. Knizhin, Irkutsk State University, pers. comm). Unregulated catches is the primary threat to the species in this region.
430|

It is suspected that the population will decrease by over 60% in the next 20 years as demand increases from China and Russia and from non-catch and release angling (Ocock _et al_. 2006). In Mongolia, fish have disappeared from rivers near town centres and downstream of mining areas. Stable populations still occur in more remote areas but these populations are vulnerable as mining, overgrazing, and fishing become more common in Mongolia. There is also illegal, international trade to China, but the scale of this trade is uncertain.
434|

Based on recent survey data, we estimate loss of range (estimated as extent of occurrence, or EOO) within Heilongjiang Province at 7% of the historic range (see Tables 1 and 2 in the Supplementary Material). 289|_**Criterion A: Population Reduction**_ Following the IUCN guidelines, we determined the overall abundance loss for this species by weighting factors. We include estimates reported in points 1–4 in the _Population_ section (below) by region (see Tables 1–3 in the additional supporting information). All range areas are calculated as extent of occurrence (EOO). Data limitations precluded us from estimating aquatic habitat area.
290|
291|Most of the historic range of the species is contained in the Russian Federation (83.8% of total). The species' historic, natural range extends into China (6.4% of total), Kazakhstan (6.1% of total) and Mongolia (3.7% of total; see Table 1 in the additional supporting information).
292|
293|We estimate a total natural range reduction of 3.6% (see Table 1 in the additional supporting information). Loss in range area for specific regions varies from 3.2% within Russia (in the Volga, Ural and Pechora Rivers), 6.9% within China (in the Amur River basin), and 19.1% within Mongolia (see Table 2 in the additional supporting information). We acknowledge that percentage loss of range calculated as area of occupancy (AOO) would likely be much higher than this, considering many populations, particularly along the southern extent of their distribution, have become significantly fragmented as a result of localized impacts from land use change and fishing pressure. However, we lack the data to generate reliable estimates of AOO for this species throughout most of its natural range.
294|
295|To arrive at a population reduction estimate for this species to evaluate it against IUCN Red List Criterion A, we used our abundance loss estimates for each region (described in points 1–4 in the _Population_ section below), weighted by the percent of the range in each region, as prescribed by the _Guidelines for Using the IUCN Red List Categories and Criteria_ (Version 9.0; see Table 3 in the additional supporting information). **Siberian taimen** (***Hucho taimen***), also known as the **common taimen** ([Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"): Обыкнове́нный тайме́нь, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Russian "Romanization of Russian"): *Obyknovénnyy tayménʹ*), **Siberian giant trout** or **Siberian salmon**, is a [species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species "Species") of [salmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmon "Salmon")-like [ray-finned fish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray-finned_fish "Ray-finned fish") from the [genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genus "Genus") *[Hucho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hucho "Hucho")* in the [family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_(taxonomy) "Family (taxonomy)") [Salmonidae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmonidae "Salmonidae"). These fish are found in rivers in [Siberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberia "Siberia") and adjacent regions, and are harvested throughout the year.

{"content": "130|The taimen is distributed from the [Volga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volga_River "Volga River") and [Pechora River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pechora_River "Pechora River") basins in the west to the [Yana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yana_(river) "Yana (river)") and [Amur River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amur "Amur") basins in the east, spanning portions of [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), [Kazakhstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakhstan "Kazakhstan"), [Mongolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolia "Mongolia"), and [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"). On a larger scale, this includes parts of the [Caspian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea "Caspian Sea"), [Arctic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Ocean "Arctic Ocean"), and [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") drainages in Eurasia. In Mongolia, the taimen is found in both the Arctic and Pacific drainages, specifically the [Yenisei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yenisei "Yenisei")/[Selenga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selenga "Selenga"), the [Lena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lena_River "Lena River"), and the Amur River Basins. The taimen lives in flowing water and is only occasionally found in lakes, usually near the mouth of a tributary. The taimen is not [anadromous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_migration "Fish migration"), but does show increased movement rates during the spawning season. The average home range size of taimen in the [Eg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eg_River "Eg River")-[Üur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Üür_River "Üür River") rivers of Mongolia is 23 kilometres (14 mi), but some tagged individuals show home ranges up to 93 kilometres (58 mi).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Some authors consider the taimen to be a subspecies of the [huchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huchen "Huchen"), i.e. *Hucho hucho taimen*.
131|
132|## Description
133|
134|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hucho_taimen&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Description")]
135|
136|Coloration varies geographically, but is generally olive green on the head blending to reddish brown in the tail. Adipose, anal, and caudal fins are often dark red. The belly ranges from nearly white to dark gray. The taimen appears to be the largest salmonid in the world, being heavier at average and maximum sizes than the largest North American salmonid, the [chinook salmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinook_salmon "Chinook salmon").[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) Most mature fish caught weigh from 15 to 30 kg (33 to 66 lb).[[6]](#cite_note-6) The average length is from 70 to 120 cm (28 to 47 in). The maximum length is about 150 to 180 cm (59 to 71 in). The maximum size is not assured, but supposedly a fish caught in the [Kotui River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kotui_River?action=edit&redlink=1 "Kotui River (page does not exist)") in Russia in 1943 with a length of 210 cm (83 in) and a weight of 105 kg (231 lb) is the largest size recorded.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The [IGFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGFA "IGFA") world record is 45.80 kg (101.0 lb) with a length of 150.00 cm (59.06 in).[[8]](#cite_note-8) It can reach at least 55 years of age.
137|
138|## Diet
139|
140|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hucho_taimen&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Diet")]
141|
142|Adult taimen are mainly [piscivores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piscivore "Piscivore"), eating fish, though they frequently eat terrestrial prey such as rodents and birds.
143|
144|## Angling and commercial use
145|
146|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hucho_taimen&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Angling and commercial use")]
147|
148|| [Fly fishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly_fishing "Fly fishing") targets |
149|| --- |
150|| * [bluefish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluefish#Gear_and_methods "Bluefish") * [brook trout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brook_trout#Angling_and_commercial_use "Brook trout") * [crappie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crappie#Angling "Crappie") * [hucho taimen](#Angling_and_commercial_use) * [largemouth bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Largemouth_bass#Angling "Largemouth bass") * [northern pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_pike#Sport_fishing "Northern pike") * [peacock bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacock_bass#Valued_as_gamefish "Peacock bass") * [shoal bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoal_bass#Sporting_Quality "Shoal bass") * [smallmouth bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallmouth_bass#Angling "Smallmouth bass") * [other sport fish...](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shad_fishing "Shad fishing") |
151|| See also |
152|| * [fishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishing "Fishing") * [Index of fishing articles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Index_of_fishing_articles "Index of fishing articles") |
153|| * [v](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:Fly_fishing_targets "Template:Fly fishing targets") * [t](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template_talk:Fly_fishing_targets "Template talk:Fly fishing targets") * [e](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Template:Fly_fishing_targets "Special:EditPage/Template:Fly fishing targets") |
154|
155|The taimen is becoming a more well-known [game fish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_fish "Game fish"), particularly for [fly fishers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly_fishing "Fly fishing"). [Catch-and-release](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catch-and-release "Catch-and-release") with [barbless hooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_hook#Points_and_barbs "Fish hook") is practised in many areas to conserve dwindling populations of this species. Private angling operators such as Mongolia River Outfitters/Fish Mongolia work with organizations such as the Wild Salmon Center's Taimen Conservation Initiative to conserve the remaining populations. While the taimen is sometimes (often illegally) harvested commercially, its low price and slow growth and reproduction make it more valuable as a game fish.
156|
157|## Conservation
158|
159|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hucho_taimen&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Conservation")]
160|
161|The taimen has been assessed as vulnerable and in decline by the [International Union for Conservation of Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Union_for_Conservation_of_Nature "International Union for Conservation of Nature") (IUCN).[[1]](#cite_note-iucn_status_19_November_2021-1) Taimen are a very sensitive species. Habitat degradation and disturbance caused by overgrazing, mining, motor boats, agriculture, and infrastructure development are primary threats. In addition, illegal fishing is a year round problem particularly in remote Mongolia. Additional challenges include the establishment of sand and gravel industries in [Heilongjiang Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heilongjiang_Province "Heilongjiang Province"), China, industrial water pollution in Europe, commercial fishing in the [Amur River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amur_River "Amur River") region of Russia and China, and illegal sport fishing throughout its range and the impacts of [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change").[[1]](#cite_note-iucn_status_19_November_2021-1) The IUCN recommends that the fish be considered for inclusion in the Convention on Migratory Species to spur international cooperation on the conservation of this fully migratory species.[[1]](#cite_note-iucn_status_19_November_2021-1)
162|
163|## Folklore
164|
165|[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hucho_taimen&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Folklore")]
166|
167|* Mongolian legend tells of a giant taimen trapped in river ice. Starving herders were able to survive the winter by hacking off pieces of its flesh. In the spring, the ice melted and the giant taimen climbed onto the land, tracked down the herders, and ate them all.
168|* According to Chinese folklore, a type of giant taimen lives in [Kanas Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanas_Lake "Kanas Lake") in China. Villagers near Kanasi claim to have found fish weighing over 4 tonnes.[[9]](#cite_note-9)
169|* *[National Geographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Geographic_(magazine) "National Geographic (magazine)")* called the taimen the "Mongolian Terror Trout".[[10]](#cite_note-10)

[Komodo National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komodo_National_Park "Komodo National Park") was founded in 1980 to protect Komodo dragon populations on islands including Komodo, Rinca, and Padar.[[92]](#cite_note-knp-92) Later, the Wae Wuul and Wolo Tado Reserves were opened on Flores to aid Komodo dragon conservation.[[17]](#cite_note-natgeo-17)

423|Volcanic activity, earthquakes, loss of habitat, fire,[[34]](#cite_note-location-34)[[17]](#cite_note-natgeo-17) tourism, loss of prey due to [poaching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poaching "Poaching"), and illegal poaching of the dragons themselves have all contributed to the vulnerable status of the Komodo dragon. A major future threat to the species is [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_in_Indonesia "Climate change in Indonesia") via both [aridification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aridification "Aridification") and [sea level rise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level_rise "Sea level rise"), which can affect the low-lying habitats and valleys that the Komodo dragon depends on, as Komodo dragons do not range into the higher-altitude regions of the islands they inhabit. Based on projections, climate change will lead to a decline in suitable habitat of 8.4%, 30.2%, or 71% by 2050 depending on the [climate change scenario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_scenario "Climate change scenario"). Without effective conservation actions, populations on Flores are [extirpated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extirpated "Extirpated") in all scenarios, while in the more extreme scenarios, only the populations on Komodo and Rinca persist in highly reduced numbers. Rapid [climate change mitigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_mitigation "Climate change mitigation") is crucial for conserving the species in the wild.[[2]](#cite_note-IUCN-2)[[93]](#cite_note-93) Other scientists have disputed the conclusions about the effects of climate change on Komodo dragon populations.[[94]](#cite_note-94)
424|
425|Under Appendix I of [CITES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CITES "CITES") (the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species), commercial international trade of Komodo dragon skins or specimens is prohibited.[[95]](#cite_note-zipcode-95)[[96]](#cite_note-96) Despite this, there are occasional reports of illegal attempts to trade in live Komodo dragons. The most recent attempt was in March 2019, when Indonesian police in the [East Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Java "East Java") city of [Surabaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surabaya "Surabaya") reported that a criminal network had been caught trying to smuggle 41 young Komodo dragons out of Indonesia. The plan was said to include shipping the animals to several other countries in Southeast Asia through Singapore. It was hoped that the animals could be sold for up to 500 million [rupiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesian_rupiah "Indonesian rupiah") (around US$35,000) each.[[97]](#cite_note-97) It was believed that the Komodo dragons had been smuggled out of [East Nusa Tenggara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Nusa_Tenggara "East Nusa Tenggara") province through the port at [Ende](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ende,_East_Nusa_Tenggara "Ende, East Nusa Tenggara") in central Flores.[[98]](#cite_note-98)
426|
427|In 2013, the total population of Komodo dragons in the wild was assessed as 3,222 individuals, declining to 3,092 in 2014 and 3,014 in 2015. Populations remained relatively stable on the bigger islands (Komodo and Rinca), but decreased on smaller islands, such as Nusa Kode and Gili Motang, likely due to diminishing prey availability.[[99]](#cite_note-99) On [Padar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padar_Island "Padar Island"), a former population of Komodo dragons has recently become extirpated, of which the last individuals were seen in 1975.[[100]](#cite_note-Lilley1995-100) It is widely assumed that the Komodo dragon died out on Padar following a major decline of populations of large [ungulate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ungulate "Ungulate") prey, for which poaching was most likely responsible.[[101]](#cite_note-SDZ-101)
428|
429|Since the species is only found in remnant populations in the Wallacean Island, studies have examined the traits and factors that led to these certain populations' surprising persistence. A comprehensive examination of the species survival suggested that rather than being a single attribute, but the a combination including ectotherm traits, varanid biology, habitat, and anthropogenic factors.[[102]](#cite_note-102)

441|Komodo dragons have long been sought-after zoo attractions, where their size and reputation make them popular exhibits. They are, however, rare in zoos because they are susceptible to infection and parasitic disease if captured from the wild, and do not readily reproduce in captivity.[[19]](#cite_note-amnh-19) A pair of Komodo dragons was displayed at the [Bronx Zoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronx_Zoo "Bronx Zoo") in New York in September 1926, but they only lasted a couple of months, dying in October and November 1926.[[103]](#cite_note-barnard-103) The first Komodo dragons were displayed at [London Zoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Zoo "London Zoo") in 1927. A Komodo dragon was exhibited in 1934 in the United States at the [National Zoo in Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Zoological_Park_(United_States) "National Zoological Park (United States)"), but it lived for only two years. More attempts to exhibit Komodo dragons were made, but the lifespan of the animals in captivity at the time proved very short, averaging five years in the National Zoological Park. Studies were done by Walter Auffenberg, which were documented in his book *The Behavioral Ecology of the Komodo Monitor*, eventually allowing for more successful management and breeding of the dragons in captivity.[[16]](#cite_note-komo-16) [Surabaya Zoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surabaya_Zoo "Surabaya Zoo") in Indonesia has been breeding Komodo dragons since 1990 and had 134 dragons in 2022, the largest collection outside its natural habitat.[[104]](#cite_note-104) As of May 2009, there were 35 North American, 13 European, one Singaporean, two African, and two Australian institutions which housed captive Komodo dragons.[[105]](#cite_note-105) In 2016, four Komodo dragons were transferred from the Bronx Zoo to [Madras Crocodile Bank Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madras_Crocodile_Bank_Trust "Madras Crocodile Bank Trust") in India.[[106]](#cite_note-106)
442|
443|A variety of behaviors have been observed from captive specimens. Most individuals become relatively tame within a short time,[[107]](#cite_note-procter-107)[[108]](#cite_note-lederer-108) and are capable of recognising individual humans and discriminating between familiar and unfamiliar keepers.[[109]](#cite_note-dragons-109) Komodo dragons have also been observed to engage in play with a variety of objects, including shovels, cans, plastic rings, and shoes. This behavior does not seem to be "food-motivated predatory behavior".[[53]](#cite_note-firefly-53)[[9]](#cite_note-sciam-9)[[110]](#cite_note-110)
444|
445|[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/At_Chester_Zoo_2023_019_-_Komodo_Dragon_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-At_Chester_Zoo_2023_019_-_Komodo_Dragon_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:At_Chester_Zoo_2023_019_-_Komodo_Dragon_(cropped).jpg)

447|Komodo Dragon at [Chester Zoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester_Zoo "Chester Zoo")
448|
449|Even seemingly docile dragons may become unpredictably aggressive, especially when the animal's territory is invaded by someone unfamiliar. In June 2001, a Komodo dragon seriously injured [Phil Bronstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Bronstein "Phil Bronstein"), the then-husband of actress [Sharon Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharon_Stone "Sharon Stone"), when he entered its enclosure at the [Los Angeles Zoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Zoo "Los Angeles Zoo") after being invited in by its keeper. Bronstein was bitten on his bare foot, as the keeper had told him to take off his white shoes and socks, which the keeper stated could potentially excite the Komodo dragon as they were the same colour as the white rats the zoo fed the dragon.[[111]](#cite_note-111)[[112]](#cite_note-112) Although he survived, Bronstein needed to have several tendons in his foot reattached surgically.[[113]](#cite_note-113)
